title: Air India Phuket-Delhi Flight Plunges 300 Feet in Severe Turbulence, Injuring 12
excerpt: An Airbus A320 carrying 134 people experienced a sudden altitude drop 90 minutes into the flight, cracking the cabin ceiling and injuring 10 passengers and two crew members.
body:
• Air India flight AI2379 from Phuket to Delhi plunged approximately 300 feet in severe turbulence on August 4, injuring 10 passengers and two crew members.
  • The Airbus A320 was cruising at altitude 90 minutes after departure when it hit a sudden pocket of turbulence, causing visible cracks in the cabin ceiling.
  • The aircraft landed safely at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport around 11 a.m., where emergency services were waiting on the tarmac.
  • All 12 injured were taken to Medanta hospital with non-serious injuries. Authorities have launched an investigation into the incident.

An Air India flight from Phuket to Delhi plunged approximately 300 feet in seconds on Monday after encountering severe turbulence over the Bay of Bengal, injuring 12 people and cracking the cabin ceiling of the Airbus A320.

Flight AI2379 was carrying 134 passengers and crew when the aircraft, cruising at altitude roughly 90 minutes after departing Thailand, hit what investigators believe was a sudden downdraft or pocket of severe clear-air turbulence. The plane dropped sharply before the crew regained control.

Chaos at Cruising Altitude

Passengers described the aircraft suddenly tilting and shaking violently for two to three minutes. Many were asleep at the time of the drop, making them especially vulnerable to being thrown from their seats.

Footage circulating on social media showed visible cracks in the cabin ceiling panels — a sign of the force with which passengers and objects struck the interior during the sudden descent. Overhead luggage bins appeared damaged, and personal belongings were scattered through the cabin.

Air India confirmed the incident, describing it as a "brief turbulence-related event while cruising" that caused a "short-lived change in altitude" before the crew brought the aircraft safely back under control. A spokesperson said passenger and crew wellbeing remained the airline's top priority.

Emergency Response at Delhi

The aircraft landed safely at Indira Gandhi International Airport just after 11 a.m. local time, where emergency services were already positioned on the tarmac. Ambulances transported the injured — ten passengers and two crew members — to the nearby Medanta medical centre in Gurugram.

Air India said none of the injuries were serious, though several passengers were seen being moved in wheelchairs upon disembarking. The airline said it was providing full support to those affected and cooperating with investigators.

A Growing Pattern

The incident adds to a concerning pattern of severe turbulence events affecting flights worldwide. Aviation experts have linked rising turbulence to climate change, with studies showing that clear-air turbulence over the North Atlantic has increased by 55% since 1979. The monsoon season in South and Southeast Asia creates particularly unpredictable atmospheric conditions, with sudden updrafts and downdrafts generated by thunderstorm cells that can catch even experienced flight crews off guard.

"The aircraft suddenly tilted and kept shaking for two to three minutes while most people on board were dozing."

— A passenger on flight AI2379

The Phuket-Delhi route, popular with Indian tourists and families returning from Thai beach holidays, traverses airspace over the Bay of Bengal and Myanmar that is particularly prone to monsoon turbulence during the July-August peak season.

Air India Under Scrutiny

The turbulence event comes at a sensitive time for Air India, which has been working to rebuild its safety reputation under the ownership of Tata Group. The airline suffered its worst disaster in decades last year when flight AI171 crashed 32 seconds after takeoff from Ahmedabad, killing 241 people on board and 19 on the ground.

While turbulence incidents are fundamentally different from mechanical failures or crashes — and are not generally considered preventable by airlines — the optics of another Air India safety event will concern a carrier still working to restore public confidence.

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has launched a probe to determine the exact circumstances of the turbulence event, including whether the flight crew had received adequate weather warnings and whether seatbelt signs were illuminated at the time of the incident.

Advice for Travellers

Aviation safety experts consistently advise passengers to keep seatbelts fastened whenever seated, even when the seatbelt sign is off. In severe turbulence events, the majority of injuries occur among unbelted passengers who are thrown from their seats. With monsoon season in full swing across South and Southeast Asia, flights on routes through this region face elevated turbulence risk through September.
